essays.stem: Plan an evaluation of a parish municipal corporation's building permit system, setting out what you would include in the terms of reference.
essays.modelAnswer: The terms of reference would begin with the background: what the permit system is, its legal and policy basis, and why it is being evaluated, for example complaints about delays. The purpose would be to judge how well the system works and to recommend improvements. The scope would cover the whole process from application to issue of the permit, including inspections and appeals, for the last two years, but would exclude the setting of fees. The evaluation questions would include: Are permits issued within the service standard? Are decisions consistent with the building rules? What does each permit cost to process? Are all applicants treated fairly? The criteria would be effectiveness, efficiency, economy and equity, with indicators such as the share of permits issued on time and the cost per permit. The methods would include analysing system data, a process map, a sample of files, a survey of applicants and interviews with staff and contractors. The terms of reference would name the evaluator and a steering group, set out confidentiality and data protection rules, and give a Gantt chart, budget and the date and format of the report.
markingPoints: Background and purpose
Clear scope, including what is excluded
Evaluation questions with criteria and indicators
Suitable mix of methods and data sources
Governance, ethics, timeline, budget and reporting

essays.stem: Compare records analysis, surveys, interviews, focus groups and observation as ways of collecting data to evaluate a public hospital's outpatient appointment system, and recommend a suitable mix.
essays.modelAnswer: Analysing the system's records, such as booking times, waiting times and no-shows, gives large amounts of objective data at low cost, but it shows what happens, not why, and depends on the data being accurate. A survey of patients can reach many people and give figures on satisfaction and waiting, but response rates may be low, and patients who cannot read well or use phones may be missed. Interviews with staff and some patients give depth and explain the reasons behind problems, but they take time and cover few people. Focus groups bring several people together to discuss issues and can reveal shared concerns, but strong voices may dominate and people may hold back in a group. Observation of the clinic on busy days shows how the system actually works, including queues and handovers, but people may act differently while being watched. I recommend starting with records analysis to find the main patterns, observing several clinic sessions, surveying a random sample of patients in person and by phone, and interviewing key staff. Using several methods allows the findings to be checked against each other.
markingPoints: Records analysis: strengths and limits
Surveys: strengths and limits, including reach
Interviews and focus groups: depth versus coverage
Observation: strengths and limits
Justified mix that allows triangulation

essays.stem: A licensing agency has two regional offices. North spent J$18,000,000 and processed 3,000 applications, 92% within the target time. South spent J$15,400,000 and processed 2,200 applications, 78% within the target time. Calculate the cost per application for each office, compare their performance and recommend what the evaluation should do next.
essays.modelAnswer: North's cost per application is J$18,000,000 ÷ 3,000 = J$6,000. South's is J$15,400,000 ÷ 2,200 = J$7,000. North is therefore more efficient, costing J$1,000 less per application, and also more effective, with 92% completed within the target time against 78% at South. On these figures, North performs better on both measures. However, the evaluation should not conclude that South is poorly managed without further evidence. The difference may come from factors such as more complex applications, larger rural areas to inspect, staff vacancies, older equipment or different ways of recording dates. The next steps would be to check that both offices record data in the same way, map the process in each office to find where time is lost, and compare a sample of files by type and complexity. Interviews with staff and a short survey of applicants in both regions would help explain the gap. If the difference is due to practices at North that could be shared, the recommendation would be to adopt them at South, with targets and a date to review progress.
markingPoints: North: J$6,000 per application
South: J$7,000 per application
Compares efficiency and effectiveness correctly
Identifies possible explanations and checks data consistency
Recommends further investigation and a practical next step

essays.stem: Explain the criteria of relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, economy, equity and sustainability, and apply them to an evaluation of a government agency's online tax payment system.
essays.modelAnswer: Relevance asks whether the system's aims still match the needs it serves. For an online payment system, it asks whether taxpayers want and need to pay online and whether the system supports the agency's goal of collecting revenue easily. Effectiveness asks whether the system achieves its intended results, such as more taxpayers paying on time and fewer errors. Efficiency compares outputs with inputs, for example the cost to the agency of each payment processed online compared with payments at the counter. Economy asks whether inputs, such as the software licence and support contract, were obtained at the lowest cost for the required quality, in line with the procurement rules. Equity asks whether all groups can use the system fairly. Older taxpayers, people in rural areas with poor internet, and people with disabilities may find it harder, so other options and help should remain. Sustainability asks whether the system will keep working after the project ends, with funds for maintenance, trained staff and security updates. Using all six criteria gives a balanced judgement rather than focusing on cost alone.
markingPoints: Relevance explained and applied
Effectiveness explained and applied
Efficiency and economy distinguished and applied
Equity explained and applied
Sustainability explained and applied, with a balanced conclusion

essays.stem: Explain the ethical responsibilities of an officer conducting an evaluation of a public body's system, and how she should meet them.
essays.modelAnswer: The evaluator must be honest and objective. Her findings should rest on evidence, and she must not change or hide results to please managers. If she has a conflict of interest, for example because she designed the system or works closely with the unit, she should declare it. She must respect the people who take part. Staff and members of the public should be told the purpose of the evaluation, how their information will be used and that taking part is voluntary, and their consent should be obtained. Where confidentiality is promised, comments should be reported as themes, without names or details that could identify someone, especially in small units. She must handle personal data in line with the data protection law: collect only what is needed, store it securely, share it only with those authorised and destroy it when no longer required. She should avoid causing harm, for example by focusing on the system rather than blaming individuals, and by treating staff fairly when findings are critical. Finally, she should report limitations openly so that decision-makers do not rely on the findings more than the evidence allows.
markingPoints: Honesty, objectivity and declaring conflicts
Informed, voluntary participation
Confidentiality in reporting
Data protection in collecting and storing data
Avoiding harm and stating limitations

essays.stem: Explain what a logic model is, and build one in words for a ministry's public complaints-handling system, showing how it would guide the evaluation.
essays.modelAnswer: A logic model is a simple chain showing how a system is meant to work: the inputs it uses, the activities it carries out, the outputs it produces, and the outcomes and longer-term impact it is meant to achieve. It helps the evaluator choose questions and indicators at each stage. For a complaints system, the inputs are complaints staff, the case management software, the complaints policy and the budget. The activities are receiving complaints by phone, email and in person, logging them, investigating, replying and analysing trends. The outputs are the number of complaints logged, investigated and answered, and the reports produced each quarter. The short-term outcomes are complainants receiving fair, timely answers and problems being fixed. The longer-term outcomes are fewer repeat complaints, improved services and greater public trust in the ministry. The evaluation would use the model to set indicators, such as the share of complaints answered within the service standard, the satisfaction of complainants and the number of service changes made because of complaints. It would also test the links, for example whether trend reports actually lead to changes.
markingPoints: Defines a logic model and its stages
Correct inputs and activities for the example
Correct outputs for the example
Short- and long-term outcomes
Shows how it guides indicators and tests links

essays.stem: Describe how an evaluator should turn the data she has collected into findings, conclusions and recommendations.
essays.modelAnswer: First, she should check the data for accuracy and completeness, removing duplicates and noting gaps. She should analyse the figures, using averages, percentages, trends and comparisons with targets, baselines and benchmarks, and present them in clear tables and charts. She should analyse interview notes, open-ended survey answers and observation notes by grouping them into themes and noting how often each appears and who raised it. Findings are the facts the evidence shows, answering each evaluation question, such as '78% of applications were completed on time, against a target of 90%'. She should check each finding against more than one source where possible. Conclusions are her judgements about what the findings mean, such as whether the system is effective, and why problems occur, using tools such as the five whys or a fishbone diagram to identify causes. Recommendations are the actions proposed to fix those causes. Each should follow from the evidence, be specific, have an owner and a date, and be realistic within the agency's resources. She should rank them by importance and note any limits in the evidence.
markingPoints: Checks data quality
Analyses quantitative and qualitative data appropriately
Findings answer the questions and are checked across sources
Conclusions judge meaning and identify causes
Specific, evidence-based, prioritised recommendations

essays.stem: Describe how you would structure the report of a systems evaluation, and how you would present the results to senior management and to the staff who run the system.
essays.modelAnswer: The report would open with a one- or two-page executive summary giving the purpose, the main findings, conclusions and the key recommendations. Next would come a short introduction with the background, scope and evaluation questions, followed by the methods used, including sample sizes, response rates and limitations. The main body would set out the findings for each evaluation question, with tables and charts and the evidence behind them, then the conclusions and the recommendations, each with a suggested owner, timeframe and cost where known. Appendices would hold the terms of reference, data tables and the survey tools. For senior management, I would hold a short briefing focused on the summary, the main risks, the costs and benefits of the recommendations, and the decisions needed, with a few clear slides. For staff who run the system, I would hold a separate session that explains the findings in plain language, credits what works well, focuses on the system rather than on individuals and invites their ideas on how to put the recommendations into practice. Both groups would receive the report in a suitable format.
markingPoints: Executive summary and introduction
Methods and limitations
Findings with evidence, conclusions and recommendations
Briefing for senior management focused on decisions
Constructive session for staff, focused on the system

essays.stem: Explain how an organisation should make sure that the recommendations of a systems evaluation are put into practice and that their effect is checked.
essays.modelAnswer: First, management should prepare a written management response to each recommendation, saying whether it is accepted, partly accepted or rejected, with reasons. Accepted recommendations should go into an action plan that sets out the specific tasks, the officer responsible, the resources needed, the start and finish dates and the indicator that will show success. The plan should be approved by senior management and, where changes affect staff or the public, explained to them. A named officer should track progress, using a simple tracker that shows each action as on track, delayed or complete, and report regularly to the senior management team or steering group. Problems, such as lack of funds or staff, should be raised early so that the plan can be adjusted. After the changes have had time to work, usually six to twelve months, the organisation should measure the agreed indicators again and compare them with the baseline taken during the evaluation. It should also collect feedback from users and staff. The results should be reported, and lessons learned should feed into future evaluations and into the organisation's planning.
markingPoints: Written management response with reasons
Action plan with owners, dates, resources and indicators
Communicating changes and tracking progress
Regular reporting and dealing with problems early
Re-measuring against the baseline and learning lessons

essays.stem: A ministry must evaluate its procurement system after public criticism. Evaluate the use of an internal team compared with an external evaluator, and recommend which it should use.
essays.modelAnswer: An internal team already knows the ministry's structure, rules and systems, so it can start quickly and at lower cost. It can find information and people easily and is more likely to remain after the evaluation to help put changes in place. However, internal staff may be too close to the system, may hesitate to criticise senior colleagues and may not be seen as independent, which is a serious weakness when the public is concerned. An external evaluator, such as an independent consultant or another public audit body, brings independence, fresh eyes and specialist knowledge of procurement and of good practice elsewhere. Its findings are more likely to be trusted by the public and by Parliament. The disadvantages are higher cost, the time needed to learn the system and the need to procure the evaluator properly. Given the public criticism, I recommend an external evaluator, appointed through a proper procurement process, with clear terms of reference. A small internal team should support the evaluator with data and access, and be involved in planning the changes, so that the ministry keeps the knowledge and ownership needed to act on the findings.
markingPoints: Advantages of an internal team
Disadvantages of an internal team, especially independence
Advantages of an external evaluator
Disadvantages of an external evaluator
Justified recommendation linked to public trust, with internal support

practical1.title: Plan a systems evaluation: terms of reference, logic model and data tools
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up public system (for example a parish municipal corporation's market vendor licensing system, a ministry's staff leave system, or a public hospital's appointment system), with a description of how it works, some complaints and some basic data. As a group, plan an evaluation and produce: terms of reference (purpose, scope, evaluation questions, criteria, governance, ethics, timeline and report date); a logic model of the system on a flipchart or slide; an evaluation matrix in a spreadsheet linking each question to its indicators, data sources and methods; a draft survey of no more than ten questions and an interview guide, each tested on another member; and a Gantt chart of the evaluation. Give each member a named role: evaluation lead (keeps time and writes the terms of reference), logic model designer, matrix builder, tools designer (survey and interview guide), and planner (Gantt chart and ethics section). In a group of four, the evaluation lead also writes the ethics section. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Case pack from the assessor describing the system, with complaints and data
Computers with word-processing and spreadsheet software
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
Templates for the terms of reference and evaluation matrix (optional)
photos: The logic model on the flipchart
The draft survey and interview guide
The tools being tested on another member
The Gantt chart of the evaluation
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Evaluation questions are clear and match the purpose
Logic model correctly separates inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes
Indicators and methods suit each question and allow checking across sources
Survey questions are clear, neutral and not leading
Ethics and data protection are properly covered
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up case and invented names
Keep the case pack and any test answers confidential
Do not collect real personal data when testing the tools
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Analyse evaluation data and present findings and recommendations
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up data pack from an evaluation of a public system: a spreadsheet of about 300 cases with dates received and completed, office and case type; survey results from users; staff interview notes; and the system's targets. As a group: calculate the key indicators (for example average processing time, the share completed within target, and the cost per case) and compare them with the targets; produce at least two clear charts; group the comments into themes; write a four-page evaluation report with an executive summary, findings, conclusions and at least four specific recommendations with owners and dates; and present the results in a ten-minute briefing to the assessor acting as the Permanent Secretary, followed by a role-played meeting to agree the management response. Give each member a named role: lead evaluator (keeps time and writes the executive summary and conclusions), data analyst (calculates the indicators), chart designer, qualitative analyst (themes from comments and interviews), and recommendations writer. In a group of four, the lead evaluator also writes the recommendations. Every member presents a part. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Made-up data pack from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet, word-processing and presentation software
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
photos: The spreadsheet showing the indicator calculations and formulas
The themes from comments on the flipchart
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Calculated the indicators correctly and compared them with targets
Charts are accurate, labelled and easy to read
Themes are drawn fairly from the comments
Findings, conclusions and recommendations are clearly separated and linked to evidence
Presented their part clearly and answered questions honestly
safety: Use only the made-up data and invented names
Keep the data pack confidential and do not identify individuals in comments
Discuss findings about the system, not blame for people
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks
